I get to have the honor of moderating this.
I want to first give you some quick ground rules.
So we have, of course, our four incredible candidates here.
They're going to answer questions from me and from Joey, Joey Bunch, from the Colorado Gazette in Colorado politics.
We're going to try to keep this very fast moving.
My first and most important request is either turn off
or at least put on airplane mode all of your cell phones.
We don't want to hear any ringing when this gets picked up.

This is also being live streamed right now as well.
So if you could do that, that would be great.
We've gotten questions from some of you and I want to thank you for that and we're going to try to get, include some of those, incorporate some of those into the program as well.
Most of all, I want to thank Ken Hibble and the El Palmar Foundation for sponsoring this.

of the El Palmar Foundation for hosting this.

But it's great to have them do this.
And what they have done for the not just Colorado Springs in El Paso County, but for the state of Colorado,
is present, thanks to them, we're able to present all eight of the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor.
So please give them both a hand.
So let's get started.
Kyle's going to start us off and we're going to get going with the official program.
And again, thank you all for being here.
Great crowd.
We all appreciate your attendance very much.
Great.
Thank you, Aaron.
Good afternoon, everyone.
And my name is Kyle Hibble, and I have the privilege of serving as president and chief operating officer for Elpe Mar Foundation.
On behalf of our trustees and the staff here at Penrose House, thank you for joining us today.
And this is such a privilege.
Since 2002, Elpe Mar's form for civic advancement has been bringing together those who are interested in the civic health of the Pikes Peak region.
We do that by holding forums, debates, panels, educational seminars.
So we encourage you to join us when we do have events such as this.
But this event is truly special.
And thanks to our partners at the Gazette and the Civic Barbecue that we're having in the
gubernatorial candidates this afternoon, and the ones who we had this morning.
We are so appreciative of their participation and the Gazette's leadership in this hopefully first of many civic barbecue events.
With that, the publisher of the Gazette, Dan Stever.
Thanks, Kyle.
And on behalf of the
And on behalf of the Gazette and Colorado politics, welcome to this first Colorado civic barbecue.

We're proud and privileged to be able to be part of this without the El Pomar Foundation in the forum, because we believe that a local newspaper done right should first and foremost be a convener, not a megaphone, but a convener of people to come together to talk about important issues.
And this year, we have an important issue to decide on.

This year, you all will be deciding who the successor is to what has been a two-term, very popular governor who presided over historic levels of economic prosperity, economic development, and prosperity for some of our citizenry.
So it's a very important election to determine what that trajectory is going to look like in the future.
It's also important because while it has been a very prosperous period of time, there are still some large, important and thorny issues that as a state we have to wrestle with.
There's some opportunities we can take advantage of and there's some people that haven't yet benefited from the economic growth that we hope we can have some of that find them.
And so this is an important event today to help you.
And that's what we hope it does.
You're here today because you care and about your future of your state.
You're also here today because you want to be informed and educated of the issues and the candidates for governor.
So welcome.
And now I'd like to introduce formally the moderator for today's show.
He is the host of an award-winning television program.
It's a bipartisan issues-oriented program, the Aaron Harbor Show.
In Denver, it's on KCDO Channel 3, it's broadcast to lots of people throughout our communities, as well as five other states.
He was recognized as the broadcaster of the year by his peers from the Colorado Broadcasting Association.
He's done countless interviews with dignitaries all from all over the world, and we're lucky to have him here today.
So with that, I'd like to formally introduce Aaron Harbor, our moderator.
Thank you very much, Dan, and thank you, Kyle, as well.
Really appreciate this opportunity.
We're going to start off with questions right away, no opening statements from the candidates, but I do want to introduce very briefly all of our candidates and thank them for being here.
And after I do introduce all four, I hope you will give them all a round of applause for
their participation in our democratic process.
And that's a little deep democratic, by the way.
Though I guess today it's a capital D. Mike Johnson, former state senator.
Carrie Kennedy, our former state treasurer.
Donna Lynn, our current lieutenant governor.
And Jared Polis, the congressman from the second congressional district.
Well, I detected tat of enthusiasm.
All right, we're going to get started right off and Joey Bunch.
I'm honored again to have Joey here from the Colorado Springs Gazette and from Colorado politics.
He's the deputy managing editor of Colorado politics veteran reporter and you should all know a Pulitzer prize winning reporter.
So Joey, take it away.
Thank you, Aaron.
I appreciate that.
You know, if I hadn't become a reporter, I think I would have been a Southern tent revival preacher.
So this makes me feel right at home today.
And I have four holy ones right next to me.
So if any of you are filled with the Spirit, just come on down to the pew and testify.
So, and I've got my colleagues from Colorado politics here.
You know, we started a year and a half, two years ago, and we've grown up fast, and we continue to grow.
Mark Hardin, our new managing editor, is here.
Mark, let him see your face.
So if you guys are mad at me, he's the guy to talk to.
Mark, you're going to be getting a lot of phone calls.
And my blood rather, Ernest Looning is here, and Ernest is going to be fact-checking today in real time.
So if any of you tell a lie, Ernest is going to alert me with a text.
So let's dive right in.
You know, one of the most important issues we're facing as a state is transportation.
And how do we pay for it?
So let's talk about that.
We heard yesterday from the Denver Metro Chamber of Commerce that they want to pass a sales tax to fund transportation.
And we've heard from the state highway department that we need $20 billion over the next 20 years to pay for this.
Where do we find a billion dollars in our budget or do you support what the Denver Metro Chamber is proposing, which is a .62% sales tax?
Let's start on the end with you, Mike, and then everybody will get a chance to answer this question.
Great, thank you all so much for being here and for coming out for some barbecue and politics.
On the transportation question, I do think I chaired the Senate Finance Committee for four years, so I can tell you we are not gonna find $20 billion in the couch cushions of the state budget.

And so I do think if we are gonna actually solve the problems that you all see every time you drive up I-25, it's gonna require going to the voters to be able to get a dedicated funding stream for transportation.
I do believe that a sales tax is the right way to do that.
I know that's challenging here in Colorado Springs because you all have already passed your own.
But we do need to do this statewide.
The benefit of a sales tax versus an income tax is you allow all of the tourists and visitors who come to Colorado to share in the burden of being able to pay for our roads and bridges.
So I think that's a better structure.
I would support going to the ballot to do that.
That would allow us to bond long term.
So I think what we have to do is, no, we're not just going to pave our way out of this problem.
You're not going to solve this one lane at a time.
We're going to have to look into mass transit, things like Hyperloop and Front Range Rail, so we can actually get people moving more efficiently rather than just keep paving more lanes.
Well, Michael, let me jump in with a follow-up here, and everybody else can address this too.
Colorado Springs has raised taxes twice now for drainage and transportation.
They're looking at 9%.
We've got communities on the western slope that are going to be paying nearly 11%.
At what point do we start breaking the backs of our communities?
There's got to be a balance here.

I think this is the hard trade off of the question is at what point do we break the backs of folks who are sitting in traffic for two and a half hours driving from Denver down to Colorado Springs to get back to their home.
And so we have to look at what's the level of services we want in the state and how do we plan to pay for those services.
And so I don't think anybody wants a two and a half hour drive to Denver anymore.

And that means one of the downsides of Tabor and Gallagher and Amendment 23, which we'll probably talk about later today, is that you've created a state where we have starved state revenue over 25 years, and you got to find a way to put that back.
Transportation is the most obvious place to start.
That's why I think the business community has raised this as a place where we got to make an impact if we're going to grow the economy.
Kerry, what do you make of that?
I mean, are you concerned about these communities that have already raised taxes, that have solved their problems?
Do we risk a, you know, what about rural communities?
I mean, it's easy to say this in the big picture, but in the micro, how do you, what do you say to people like Colorado Springs?
Yeah, Joey, we need a statewide solution on transportation.
We've been following behind for decades.
40% of the state's lane miles today are rated in poor condition.
And as a mom, trying to get home after work, I know too many families in this state aren't able to get home to have dinner with their kids because they get stuck in traffic.
We have an adequately prepared for or manage the growth that we have on the front range today.
So it's going to take leadership to make the investments in our transportation systems, both here on the front range and statewide.
to support our economic growth and prosperity so it reaches throughout the state and to make sure that we're not all sitting in traffic.
So I applaud the chamber for working on moving a proposal to the ballot to increase revenue for transportation in our state.
We've been held back for decades and it is holding our state's economy back.
Donnie, you've seen the front row.
You've had a front row seat to the politics of all this for the last couple of years.
What's your answer?
Well, I think the first thing to recognize is Colorado, in spite of the pain of going from where we are to another place, we are a relatively low tax statement.
You look at studies like the Tax Foundation.
That's number one.
And we're a pretty wealthy state as well.
The second thing that everybody should recognize is that, yes, the administration and partnership with the legislature
took a very big step this year to add over the next two years, $645 million out of the general fund unprecedented because that's not generally where we spend our road money.
So recognizing this isn't just about putting a burden on you as individual taxpayers and as through a sales tax, $645 million is going to get a good start on some of the work that we need to do.
The third piece is we've got to talk about more than just roads.

And many of us will say, you build a lane, we're going to fill it up, but we have some mass transit solutions that we've got to continue to focus on in this state and bring us into the places where many other urban areas are.
Jared, you've heard their answers.
How's your answer different?
I want to first thank El Pomar and the Gazette for holding this forum.
You know, when you look at the cost of doing nothing, $600 per driver per year in gas and vehicle damage and productivity loss in traffic,
We simply can't afford that kind of competitive hit against our economy.
We need to do more alternatives.
It's not just about lane expansion.
It's about front-range rail, public and foreign columns.
That's about increased bus and bike and rapid transit.
And yes, it's about affordable housing so people can live closer to where they work, recognizing those savings on the front end.
Finally, we need to make sure that we include in the infrastructure package a high-speed internet connectivity in rural broadband.
We need to interconnect all of Colorado, enabling telecommuting, getting cars off our road and telemedicine, which can be life-saving in many of our rural communities.
Okay, so one of the really interesting issues is in terms of funding this.
Currently, our gasoline sales tax has not been increased since roughly 1991, 1992.
It's at 18 cents a gallon.
If it were simply adjusted for inflation to buy another, whatever, 18, 19 cents, that would provide the revenue to bond, for the state to bond, the money it needs at a rate of
$20 billion a billion a year for 20 years to repair all the roads that need repair to fix all the bridges that need to be fixed and to expand roadways to accommodate growing population.
Jared, starting with you.
So would you be in favor of that as a solution?
So now that you're talking about potential solutions, I'm open to a wide variety of them.
And the role as governor, you have to work with the business community, Democrats, and Republicans to find the best one to advance.
Like many, that would require a vote of the people.

So when it comes down to how we fund it, how we fix it, I think it's important to have a governor that's not wedded to any one particular idea that's willing to embrace a coalition around going to the ballot to get the funds we need to build a 21st century infrastructure to allow our state to succeed.
So would you support that kind of effort?
I would consider that absolutely an option that we would consider.
Again, I'm not saying that's my proposal, but it's one that I would be open to talking about.
All right, Donna, what's your response?
I think there's often not in this room, because I know everybody's pretty smart in this room, but there's a perception that bonding somehow is free.
And it isn't.

We pay interest on the bond, so therefore we're paying more to borrow, whereas I think the sales tax and the money that was put aside in the state's budget this year, and there's an ongoing commitment as well beyond the next two years, is a current-day commitment to doing what we need to do.
The problem with the gas tax is
More and more, we have fuel efficient vehicles.
We're getting greater mileage.
And by the way, most of us up here, I think, agree.
We'd like to see a place where we move to electric vehicles.
And so therefore, there isn't gas.
I myself drive a hybrid, and I fill up maybe three times a week because I'm using that hybrid vehicle power.
And that's what we've got to move to in this state and get away from the reliance on fossil fuels, whether it's for gas or it's for other purposes.
So Carrie, where do you come out on this issue of the gasoline tax and adjusting it for inflation?
So what we do going forward can't mirror what we've done in the past.
For 100 years, we've used the fuel tax as our primary source of funding to fund our transportation networks across the state.
And ever since the table amendment passed been almost 25 years, the fuel tax has eroded
By half, we have the purchasing power.
That's half of the projects, half of the infrastructure, half of the lane miles that we can invest in.

And as cars become more fuel efficient, and we are all hopeful that over the next several decades that we are able to move to clean, renewable sources of power in the transportation sector, we have to look at alternatives.
We have to look at new ways of financing our infrastructure, and we can't just
widen our way out of traffic.
We have to think broadly about mobility and transit.
It is time for high-speed passenger rail along the I-25 corridor.
Colorado's population is forecasted to double again.
It's doubled in my lifetime.
We have to be thinking about the future.
Mike, please.
And by the way, in terms of applause, it's fine.
But keep in mind, if you're applauding while a candidate is talking, then the TV viewers will hear your applause, but they will not hear your candidate's response.
So be thoughtful about when you applaud.
Thank you.
Thank you.
I think one of the things that I believe is you deserve direct answers to questions.
So the answer is no.
I would not support a gas tax.
And here's why, which is if you look at the major vehicle producers in the country, GM has said in the next five years, they will stop making gas vehicles altogether.
They're going to do all electric fleets.
So what you know is you would be, that might sound like a good short-term solution, but in three, five years, the state would be broke again with no revenue source from a gas tax.
And so you have three basic strategies.
You could do gas tax.
You could do income.
You could do sales.
Gas is going to run out in five years because it won't be enough gas.
Income is going to disproportionately hurt Colorado residents because tourists pay no part of it, which leaves you with sales as the best compromise.
It doesn't mean it's great, but it means it spreads the cost among tourists as well as locals.
I was very proud of the fact that I
sponsored the bill to provide a tax credit for electric vehicles.
Colorado is now the best state in the country to buy an electric vehicle, and that's great news.
That means we'll move more and more quickly towards cleaner energy, and that's why I've proposed moving to 100% renewable energy on the electric grid.
But when we do that, that means there'll be less gas being consumed and less gas tax to collect.
All right, thank you, Mike.
Joey.

Well, we're going to ask each of the candidates an individual question, something that we think that your voters deserve to hear an answer from, and a question that's going to make you hate me and this audience want to kill me.
And I'd just like to say that Ernest Looning helped me write these questions.
That's a camera, Ernest.
Mike, you've staked a major plank of your campaign is anti-gun violence.
And in 2013, you sponsored two of the three bills and only sponsored those bills late in the process.
How does that qualify as standing up to the NRA?
Isn't that really just jumping on the bandwagon?

You can ask Senator Guzman or anybody who served in the Senate with me and they will tell you that I was the first and maybe the only Senate Democrat who spoke on the floor of the Senate to fight for this bill.
You can check the front page of the Denver Post.

You can see that I'm someone who's both own guns my whole life and was the early one to stand up and say yes we have to do background checks and yes we have to make sure that we ban high-capacity magazines.
I'm the only one on this stage who has fought the NRA twice and won twice, so I would probably put my record up against anybody in this space.
And you can call any of the Republicans who fought against me on that bill and ask them who was the one in the well-fighting them tooth and nail to that entire battle.
And I guarantee you the first name they'll give you is Mike Johnson.
But what was your hesitancy?
Why didn't you sponsor the bills initially or carry one of the bills?
Well, I didn't have any hesitancy.
As you know, the way bills get introduced, a certain member decides to carry it.
In this case, the Senate President carried several of them.
So once they get introduced, you don't get to add yourself as a co-sponsor often until after the vote.
And so that was when I did that.
But there was no doubt on where I stood.
I fought early and hard and effectively, I think, to get those passed.
I'm very proud of that.
Kerry, let me ask you a question, and it's not did Mike Johnson show leadership against the NRA.
Your question is this, it's the obvious, which means obviously I'm going to ask it.
You lost to Walker Stapleton eight years ago as the incumbent, and I think most Democrats believe Walker Stapleton will be the nominee.
Why should Democrats think you'll do better this time around?
Because I'm going to beat him in the governor's race.
Yeah, Walker and I had a good campaign and he won that election 2010 was a tough year nationally for Democrats running for office.
And I also, you know, often say you have to lose in order to learn how to win.
And I learned a lot during that campaign, and I'm running this campaign differently.
I'm spending a lot more time listening, a lot more time meeting with folks in their own communities, and hearing what the diverse issues are across this state.
I believe the issues that I've prioritized in this campaign that I've worked on my entire career, which is building a public education system that we can all be proud of in this state.
and managing and addressing growth so that we protect our beautiful state and keep Colorado the place that we love.
Those are the issues that are on the top minds of voters across the state.
Donna Jared, we'll come back to you guys.
Donna and Jared don't get individual questions.
They have no skeletons in their closet.
Nothing to worry about.
No, we will come back to you.
This is a question for everybody.
I'd like to get just a half minute answer in response.
Colorado is a personal property tax on business.
And if you look at the amount of revenue collected by business or on businesses,
versus their actual cost of complying with that business, many estimates say that the cost that businesses incur is greater than the revenues collected by the state.
So my question is, would you be in favor of eliminating the personal property tax on businesses?
And if so, how would you backfill or replace that revenue?
So, Jared, I'm going to start with you.
So, and I think what we often call the tax you're referring to as the use tax, is that the same tax as I always called it.

No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no,
than it actually generates for the state.
And any thought about how you would replace that revenue, because in certain communities, that's actually a significant amount of revenue.
Yeah, again, you have to look at where the savings are from not having that tax.

So if, again, if the tax costs more than it raises, if you eliminate the tax, you say, well, where are those savings and how do we capture part of those for the public sector, allowing the private sector to keep the surplus, resulting in a net gain for both the taxpayers and for the businesses?
Donna, please.
Well, I'm a little uncomfortable talking about eliminating attacks.
And one of the things that we've identified are the huge needs that this state has that are limited by whether it's TABER, Amendment 23 Gallagher.
We've got some real issues here in terms of providing services to everyday Coloradans.
And before we eliminate attacks, we've got to answer the what do we do about it.
And quite frankly, I think you all deserve a complete overhaul of our tax structure.
and our way that we have amended our constitution by just throwing things over the fence and not thinking thoughtfully.
Thank you very much.
Kerry, please.
So we have to make sure that Colorado's business tax climate is competitive.
We want our businesses here to be successful.
We need to make sure our tax policies keep our state affordable for families.
The business personal property tax is onerous, particularly on small businesses, and it piles on another challenge for businesses doing in our state, which is the Gallagher amendment.
So you're going to see me work as I have throughout my entire career.
to reform our tax structure, to make sure that we can adequately support our state services, but do it in a way that keeps our businesses competitive and our state affordable.
Thank you, Kerry.
Mike, please.
So I own a small business, my family does, and so I can tell you we pay this property tax, and it is onerous.

I will also tell you you're going to get Mayor Souther's a heart attack, because having been the chair of the finance committee that oversees this, the business personal property tax is the major source of revenue for local governments and local towns and cities.
And so we've tried several times, and I've worked with Republicans to try to reduce this.
And what you find is that if you don't backfill that with some other source of income, you're going to have a profound impact on local government.
I would not support repealing the business personal property tax.
I think if you wanted to replace it with either income or sales, you'd have to have voters willing to do that.
But I think absent that, you'll cut off funding to local communities and you won't have a backfill because Gallagher has taken so much of that revenue out.
All right, speaking of taxes and tax credits, Colorado has a very generous tax credit for electric vehicles.
I think it's about $5,000.
You're going to get this one first, too, Mike.
And of course, federal governments at 7,500, does it make sense to have that kind of tax credit, that kind of cash credit for purchases of electric vehicles, especially given the fact that
If you look at who takes advantage of them, it certainly is a rule, not people at the lower end of the financial scale.
So what's your thought on that?
My thought is obviously, yes, because I sponsored that bill.
And so the reason why is when you look at the impact on the rest of the state, it is better to move as many people as we can
on to electric vehicles.
It means both you reduce emissions, which decreases impact on the ozone, slows down climate change, also keeps Colorado's environment cleaner.
It can reduce healthcare costs long term.
It can reduce utility bills.
The key is, of course, that means when you plug that electric vehicle in,
You want to make sure that electric vehicle is also being plugged in to a grid that's renewable.
That's why I propose moving the electric grid towards 100% renewable energy so that you're pulling wind and solar energy off that grid and not coal and gas.
If you plug an electric car into an outlet that's sending you coal, you're not a lot better off than if you plug one in, if you use natural gas directly.
But I think electric vehicles combined with renewable energy and the electric grid sends Colorado into the future in a way that makes us both the cleanest state and the most economically competitive.
Kerry, what's your take on that tax credit?
I also support tax credits for electric vehicles.

Climate change is the most pressing issue of our lifetimes, of our children's lifetimes, and we need to move aggressively to convert our power systems from fossil fuels to clean, renewable sources of energy.
And we know nationally, now that the transportation sector is the leading cause of CO2 emissions into the atmosphere.
So all of us need to work together
to make gains in the transportation sector to increase the availability of electric vehicles.
I am thrilled that Colorado is using the settlement money from the Volkswagen settlement to expand electric vehicle charging stations.

every 50 miles on our highways were in consortium with other western states so that people know that when they purchase their electric vehicles that they have the range that they need to be able to drive.
And I sure hope by the time my grandchildren, I don't have grandkids, but I hope by the time my grandkids are buying cars that we are at 100% electric on our roads.
All right, thank you, Kerry.
Donna, what's your perspective on this?
of agreement across all of us on this issue and certainly not every electric vehicle is out of the pocketbook of people.
I was looking up on Nissan Leaf the other day and I think they're pretty affordable for most people.
So we've got to continue I believe that tax credit and we also have to do the work that I and a lot of others have been doing in our own state government with the Colorado Energy Office and thanks.

to the legislature this year for stepping up and funding that office because I was the person that had to go tell 35 employees that they may not have jobs to do the work that we all deserve to really figure out our future.

And on electric charging stations, we have built not just a statewide grid, but we're building a regional grid because you certainly don't want to be driving your electric vehicle to Utah and find out there's no way to charge it.
We've had some great success in building a regional approach to how we continue to support the expansion of electric vehicles.
Thank you, Donna.
Jared, you get the last word on this issue.
Yes, I support support for electric vehicles, but it's not enough.
I also support raising the vehicle emissions standard for cleaner air.
Colorado should be on the forefront along with other states in the absence of leadership from Washington and from Trump going backwards.

We also built into my transportation plan at PolisforColorado.com, Electric Vehicle Infrastructure, making sure that that's part of the investment we make to make electric vehicles a reality across our state.
We also want to move quickly to 100% renewable energy.

We have a plan to transition our state to 100% renewable energy by 2040 or sooner, creating good green jobs that can't be outsourced, saving you money, cleaner air, doing our part on climate, and yes, making sure that we charge electric vehicles with power from a green grid.
Okay, I'm gonna ask one more energy related question in this arena and then turn it over to Joey.

Three government entities, the city of Boulder, the county of Boulder, and San Miguel County in Colorado recently filed a climate change suit against Suncor and ExxonMobil claiming that those companies misled citizens and the government about the effects, the ill effects, the climate change, and it's seeking billions of dollars in damages.
Is this a waste of taxpayer money or is this a good idea?
Jared, I'm going to start with you.
I'm not an attorney.
What I'm excited about at the local level is when I launched my campaign in Pueblo, we highlighted Pueblo City's commitment to 100% renewable energy by 2035.
They were joined by Pueblo County, the second county in Colorado just a couple weeks ago to commit to 100% by 2035, Summit County.
Over, I think 11 municipalities is what we're at now across our state with bold renewable energy goals.
And again, in the absence of leadership out of Washington,
with Trump going the wrong way, pulling out of Paris and going backwards.
We need local communities, cities, counties, and yes, the state with our statewide plan for 100% renewable energy by 2040.
I'm proud to be backed by the Sierra Club to get that done.
So lawsuits may occur.
Lawyers will debate them.
They'll get paid.
Judges will decide.
But at the end of the day, I'm so excited by the ground law of support at the local level.
So do you support this lawsuit?
Would you say you're for it or against it?
Lawsuits aren't a political matter.
So I mean, again, I have there's been lawsuits I filed amicus briefs in in the past and I'm happy to talk about those, but I haven't intervened in this law in this lawsuit.
OK, Donna.

So I think why Colorado needs a strong and experienced governor is because while I respect local control, these are issues that a governor who can bring people together can tackle and can tackle collaboratively.
So whether it's differences in minimum wage, difference in where we
put our oil and gas drilling.
These are things that, quite frankly, there's a cost to the business community.
There's a cost to you as taxpayers if we continue to behave like there isn't a central figure in the state.
And there is.
That's a governor.
That's a governor who has the credibility
